title: Scaling from zero to millions of users
subtitle: Most systems grow through the same few steps, from one server to many parts. Learn the usual order, what makes each step worth it, and why you should measure before you add anything.

c.v: This story is made up, but it is common. A small team builds a ticket booking app. It runs on one server: the web app and the database together. For a year this works fine.
Then the team plans for growth. In one quarter they add Kafka, a Redis cluster, six
microservices
and a
sharded
database. They have 3,000 daily users.

A popular concert goes on sale. The site slows to a crawl. The team looks at the dashboards they have, and none of them show the problem. After two days of searching, they find it. One slow SQL query with no index was reading the whole bookings table on every page load.
The new parts did not help. They made the system harder to debug, and nobody had measured anything before adding them. One index fixed the problem.
Scaling is not a list of tools to install. It is a series of answers to problems you can see in your numbers.
A well-known chapter of ByteByteGo's System Design Interview course walks one system from a single user to millions, one step at a time.
The steps are not a law. Treat them as a typical order: in our experience, each step fixes the most likely next bottleneck.
The rule behind every step:
find what is full, then fix only that.
The chapter ends by saying that scaling a system is an iterative process.
The key idea.
Each part you add fixes one kind of limit and adds new ways to fail. Add a part when a measurement says you need it, not because big companies have it.
Step through how the system grows. Use Next and Back, or the ← and → keys.
0. Measure from day one
Before any step, you need numbers. The Google SRE book names
four golden signals
latency
, traffic, errors and saturation. If you can measure only four
metrics
of a user-facing system, measure these.
Saturation tells you what is full. Latency and errors tell you if users feel it. Use
back-of-envelope estimates
to guess what will fill up next.
1. One server
At the start, everything runs on one server.
It is cheap and easy to debug. Its weakness: if that server goes offline, users cannot reach the site.
2. A separate database
Move the database to its own machine.
Now the app and the database stop fighting for the same CPU and memory, and you can size each one on its own.
Trigger (our advice):
the app and the database compete for CPU, memory or disk on one machine.
3. Bigger machine, or more machines?
Vertical scaling
means a bigger machine: more CPU and RAM.
Horizontal scaling
means more machines. When traffic is low, vertical scaling is a good choice because it is simple.
But it has a hard limit, and one machine gives you no
failover
AWS's reliability advice is to replace one large resource with several small ones, so one failure hurts less.
Trigger (our advice):
scale up first while it is cheap. Scale out when you near the largest machine, or when one machine going down is not acceptable.
4. A load balancer and stateless app servers
A
load balancer
spreads requests across several app servers.
For this to work, the app servers must be
stateless
. Move session data out of server memory into a shared store, so any server can handle any request.
See
Load balancing
for how the balancer picks a server.
Trigger:
one app server is near its CPU limit, or you need to survive one server dying.
5. Read replicas
Many apps read far more than they write. With replication, the main database takes the writes and
replicas
serve the reads.
Replicas can lag behind the main database, so a user may not see their own write at once. See
Replication
Trigger:
database CPU is high and most queries are reads. Check first that slow queries are not the real cause.
6. A cache
A
cache
keeps often-read data in memory, so fewer reads reach the database.
It adds new problems: stale data and many requests missing at once. See
Caching and cache stampedes
Trigger:
the same data is read again and again, and it can be a little out of date.
7. A CDN for static files
A
CDN
is a network of servers spread around the world that serves static content, such as images, CSS and JavaScript.
Users get files from a nearby server, and your servers do less work. See
CDNs and HTTP caching
Trigger:
static files use much of your
bandwidth
, or users far away see slow page loads.
8. Queues for slow work
Some work does not need to finish before you reply to the user. In the chapter's example, web servers put photo processing jobs on a
message queue
, and workers do them in the background.
The queue also lets the two sides scale and fail on their own. See
Queues vs logs
Trigger:
a request waits on slow work, such as sending email or resizing images, that the user does not need to see at once.
9. Sharding
Replicas help with reads. They do not help when one database cannot take all the writes or hold all the data. Then you split the data across shards, each with a part of the rows.
Sharding is hard to undo, and queries across shards get harder. See
Sharding and consistent hashing
Figma is a real example of this order. In 2020 it ran one Postgres database on AWS's largest physical instance.
By the end of 2022 it had added caching, read replicas and a dozen databases split by table.

It moved to horizontal sharding only when some tables reached several terabytes and billions of rows. Their writes would also soon pass the IOPS limit of Amazon RDS. Its first sharded table shipped in September 2023.
Trigger:
writes or data size on one database near its limits, after indexes, query fixes, replicas and splitting tables are done.
After that
The chapter goes further, to several data centers.
See
Multi-region systems
when you get there.
Bigger machine
More CPU and memory, with no code change.
A hard size limit. Still one point of failure.
Separate database
The app and database stop fighting for resources.
One more machine and one network hop.
Load balancer and stateless servers
More traffic. One server can die safely.
Sessions must move to a shared store.
Read replicas
Read load on the database.
Replica lag. Users may read old data.
Cache
Repeated reads of hot data.
Stale data, stampedes, one more system to run.
CDN
Static file load and distance to users.
Purging old files. Cost per GB.
Queue
Slow work blocking requests.
Duplicates, retries, a backlog to watch.
Sharding
Write load and data size on one database.
Cross-shard queries, resharding, hot keys. Hard to undo.
Simple rule (our advice):
go down this table only as far as your numbers force you to.

sections.name: At work
sections.title: At work: how a senior uses this

c.v: Ask
"What is full?"
before any scaling proposal. Ask for the graph that shows it.
Fix the cheap things first: a missing index, an N+1 query, a bigger instance.
Write the trigger down. For example: "We add a read replica when database CPU stays above 70% at peak." Then the decision is not a debate later.
Make app servers stateless early. It is cheap when the code is small and painful later.
For each new part, ask who runs it, how it fails and how you will see it fail.
Use the AWS principle "stop guessing capacity": watch demand and add or remove resources to match it.
Remember that cloud
quotas
still apply.
Plan for
load tests
and
capacity planning
before big events, not after.
"Here are our dashboards for latency, traffic, errors and CPU, memory and disk for each machine. Which resource is closest to full at peak? What is the cheapest change that buys us 3x headroom?"
"Find any place where this app keeps user state in server memory, such as sessions, uploads on local disk or in-process caches. List what must move before we run more than one server."
"List the 10 slowest database queries from this log, with how often each runs. Suggest an index or query change for each, before we talk about replicas."
The agent's plan starts from a measured bottleneck, not from a standard diagram.
It did not suggest sharding or microservices when an index or a bigger machine would do.
Any proposed cache says how data is kept fresh and what happens on a miss.
Each new part comes with the metric that shows it works and an alert for when it fails.
Cost is in the plan. More parts mean more servers to pay for and more
on-call
work.
Every step after the first one turns your app into a distributed system. Read
Why distributed systems are hard
next. For reads and writes in depth, see
Scaling reads
and
Scaling writes and hot keys

q.v: Your one database server is at 90% CPU, and most of its queries are reads of the same popular pages. What is a good next step?

options.v: Add a cache or a read replica for those reads.

why.v: The trigger is read load on hot data. A cache or replica fixes that at a much lower cost than sharding.

q.v: Why must app servers be stateless before you put many of them behind a load balancer?

options.v: So any server can serve any user, and losing one server loses no sessions.
Load balancers only work with stateless servers.

why.v: Move sessions to a shared store. Then the load balancer can send each request anywhere, and servers can come and go.

q.v: What is the main limit of vertical scaling?

options.v: It is slower to set up than horizontal scaling.
There is a largest machine you can buy, and one machine is still one point of failure.
It does not work with databases.

why.v: The ByteByteGo chapter says vertical scaling has a hard limit and gives no failover or redundancy.

q.v: Which four signals does the Google SRE book say to measure first for a user-facing system?

why.v: These are the four golden signals. They tell you which step you need next.
